If you downgrade to **Free**, you **lose access to the GPT Builder and any GPTs you created** (they are *not deleted*, but you can’t use/edit them until you upgrade again). citeturn0search1

Adobe has made a surprising move by integrating key creative tools — Photoshop, Adobe Express, and Acrobat — directly into ChatGPT, allowing users to access and use these applications for free within the AI platform. The integration simplifies the interface, making it easier to apply edits and effects without needing to learn the full applications.

To access the tools, users link their Adobe account with ChatGPT. However, this integration involves a trade-off: Adobe gains access to user data, such as conversation history, IP addresses, and location information, which could be used for marketing and data analytics. Despite data privacy concerns, the partnership boosts ChatGPT’s competitiveness—especially against Google's image generation tools—while promoting Adobe’s reach to ChatGPT’s large user base of an estimated 800 million weekly users.

Pinned chats help address the common issue of losing conversations in a long, disorganized list, especially when they’re auto-named. 

To pin a chat, users on the web can hover over a chat title, click the three-dot menu, and select "Pin." On mobile, they can press and hold a chat to access the option. However, a limitation exists: only up to three chats can be pinned at a time. Additionally, users can rename chats to make them easier to locate. While not the most exciting update, pinned chats effectively enhance user experience by improving conversation management.

entries.title: OpenAI is storing deleted ChatGPT conversations as part of its NYT lawsuit
entries.snippet:
OpenAI announced that it is being compelled to indefinitely retain deleted ChatGPT conversations following a court order tied to The New York Times' copyright lawsuit against the company. The order, issued last month, requires OpenAI to preserve all output log data, even if users request deletion or privacy laws mandate its erasure. OpenAI, which previously retained deleted chats for only 30 days, is now forced to halt this policy pending further legal direction.

This mandate affects free, Pro, Plus, and Team ChatGPT users, but not those using ChatGPT Enterprise, ChatGPT Edu, or businesses with zero data retention agreements. OpenAI assures that the stored data will remain non-public and only accessible to a small, audited team for legal purposes.

OpenAI COO Brad Lightcap and CEO Sam Altman have criticized the court order as a privacy overreach, pledging to appeal it and protect user privacy. The New York Times, which sued OpenAI and Microsoft in 2023 for allegedly using its content to train AI models, argues the data retention is essential to preserve evidence for their case. The Times has not commented on the situation.

entries.title: OpenAI is storing deleted ChatGPT conversations as part of its NYT lawsuit
entries.snippet:
OpenAI announced that it is being compelled to indefinitely retain deleted ChatGPT conversations following a court order tied to The New York Times' copyright lawsuit against the company. The order, issued last month, requires OpenAI to preserve all output log data, even if users request deletion or privacy laws mandate its erasure. OpenAI, which previously retained deleted chats for only 30 days, is now forced to halt this policy pending further legal direction.

This mandate affects free, Pro, Plus, and Team ChatGPT users, but not those using ChatGPT Enterprise, ChatGPT Edu, or businesses with zero data retention agreements. OpenAI assures that the stored data will remain non-public and only accessible to a small, audited team for legal purposes.

OpenAI COO Brad Lightcap and CEO Sam Altman have criticized the court order as a privacy overreach, pledging to appeal it and protect user privacy. The New York Times, which sued OpenAI and Microsoft in 2023 for allegedly using its content to train AI models, argues the data retention is essential to preserve evidence for their case. The Times has not commented on the situation.

entries.title: Your ChatGPT chats could be less private than you thought - here's what a new OpenAI court ruling means for you
entries.snippet: A recent U.S. court ruling requires OpenAI to hand over 20 million ChatGPT logs as part of an ongoing lawsuit with The New York Times, which accuses OpenAI of using its content without permission to train its AI systems. Magistrate Judge Ona Wang stated that privacy protections are in place and ordered OpenAI to anonymize the data before submission. While OpenAI claims that this move threatens user privacy and trust, they are appealing the decision. The historical data in question spans from December 2022 to November 2024 and might include conversations from that period, though OpenAI asserts all identifying information has been removed. The ruling marks a significant shift in AI data privacy expectations, raising concerns about user confidentiality in legal contexts. Although new data isn’t required to be preserved, this case is a stark reminder of the potential exposure of personal information shared with AI systems, signaling future privacy challenges in the AI landscape.

entries.title: ChatGPT is back following global outage - here's what happened
entries.snippet:
On June 10, 2025, ChatGPT experienced a major global outage that disrupted access for users across North America, Europe, the UK, Australia, and beyond, lasting over 10 hours. Both the free and paid ChatGPT services, as well as the AI video and image tool Sora, were affected. Reports began surfacing early morning via DownDetector, peaking at nearly 2,000 outage complaints, before gradually declining.

OpenAI confirmed it was aware of the issue and later identified the root cause, though no specific technical details were disclosed. The problem led to elevated error rates, long latency, or total non-responsiveness. Subscribers to ChatGPT Plus were not immune, and many professionals and students dependent on the tool for work experienced disruptions.

Workarounds were eventually discovered — such as accessing the o3 model — and OpenAI implemented a fix late in the day. As the outage subsided, usage gradually resumed, albeit with continued monitoring and isolated issues. During the downtime, alternatives like DeepSeek, Claude, and Gemini saw a surge in interest as users sought backup tools. OpenAI has not confirmed any compensation for affected paid users. By June 11, service had largely returned to normal.
